es.summary: Inflamación de los senos paranasales, generalmente por infección viral o bacteriana, que produce obstrucción del drenaje y dolor facial. Puede ser aguda (<4 sem), subaguda (4‑12 sem), crónica (>12 sem) o recurrente.
key_points: Obstrucción del drenaje mucoso produce presión y dolor facial
Fiebre y secreción purulenta sugieren etiología bacteriana
Diagnóstico se basa en historia, examen físico y, de ser necesario, TC sinusal
Tratamiento incluye antibiótico, descongestionante y medidas locales
Complicaciones graves: celulitis orbital, absceso subdural, meningitis

pathophysiology: Infección o irritante causa inflamación de la mucosa sinusal
Mucosa inflamada produce edema y aumenta la viscosidad del moco
Obstrucción del ostio impide el drenaje al nasofaringe
Acumulación de secreción genera presión y dolor
Si persiste, puede haber necrosis y extensión a estructuras adyacentes
risk_factors: Desviación del tabique o pólipos nasales
signs_symptoms: Dolor facial localizado (frente, mejillas) que empeora al inclinarse
Congestión nasal y secreción espesa (purulenta o amarilla)
diagnostics: Exploración física: sensibilidad a la palpación de los senos
Rinorrea purulenta y edema de mucosa nasal
TC de senos paranasales: opacificación y engrosamiento mucoso
CBC: leucocitosis con neutrofilia si es bacteriana
Cultivo de secreción nasal solo si se sospecha patógeno resistente
treatment: Antibiótico de amplio espectro (p. ej. amoxicilina, cefdinir) si se sospecha bacteriana
Descongestionante oral o tópico (p. ej. pseudoefedrina, oximetazolina)
Analgesia: paracetamol o ibuprofeno para dolor y fiebre
Irrigación nasal con solución salina isotónica
Corticoide nasal tópico (fluticasona) en casos crónicos
nursing_care: Evaluar dolor facial usando escala de 0‑10 y localizar zona de sensibilidad
Monitorear temperatura y signos de infección sistémica
Mantener hidratación adecuada (≥ 2 L/día) para fluidificar secreciones
Posicionar al paciente semi‑Fowler para favorecer drenaje
Aplicar compresas tibias en zona frontal/malar 10‑15 min, 3‑4 veces/día
patient_teaching: Realizar irrigación nasal con solución salina dos veces al día
Evitar exposición a humo, polvo y alérgenos
Completar el ciclo completo de antibiótico aunque mejore antes
Usar humidificador en ambiente seco y descansar adecuadamente
Buscar atención si empeora fiebre, visión borrosa o dolor ocular

evidenced_by: sensación de presión en frente y mejillas
outcomes: Alivio del dolor reportado ≤3/10 en 48 h
Disminución de la necesidad de analgésicos en 72 h

interventions.action: Administrar analgésico según prescripción y evaluar efecto en 30 min
interventions.rationale: Controlar la intensidad del dolor y prevenir la respuesta inflamatoria

interventions.action: Aplicar compresa tibia en zona frontal/malar 10‑15 min, 3‑4 veces/día
interventions.rationale: Facilita la vasodilatación y reduce la presión sinusoidal

interventions.action: Enseñar al paciente técnicas de relajación y uso de analgésico PRN
interventions.rationale: Promueve autocontrol del dolor y uso adecuado de medicación

interventions.action: Revaluar escala de dolor cada 2 h y registrar cambios
interventions.rationale: Permite ajustar intervenciones y detectar mejoría o deterioro

interventions.action: Mantener hidratación oral de al menos 2 L/día
interventions.rationale: Ayuda a fluidificar secreciones y disminuir irritación

outcomes: No se presenten signos de infección secundaria en 7 días
Temperatura ≤37.5 °C durante el periodo de riesgo

interventions.action: Monitorear temperatura cada 4 h y registrar valores
interventions.rationale: Detección temprana de fiebre indica posible infección secundaria

interventions.action: Observar y describir la cantidad y color de la secreción nasal
interventions.rationale: Cambios en la secreción pueden señalar progresión infecciosa

interventions.action: Educar al paciente sobre la importancia de completar el antibiótico prescrito
interventions.rationale: Previene recaídas y resistencia bacteriana

interventions.action: Instruir en higiene nasal con solución salina dos veces al día
interventions.rationale: Facilita eliminación de patógenos y reduce colonización

interventions.action: Fomentar evitar irritantes (humo, polvo) y mantener ambiente humidificado
interventions.rationale: Disminuye la irritación de la mucosa y el riesgo de infección

en.summary: Inflammation of the paranasal sinuses, usually due to viral or bacterial infection, causing obstruction of drainage and facial pain. It can be acute (<4 weeks), subacute (4‑12 weeks), chronic (>12 weeks) or recurrent.
key_points: Obstruction of mucous drainage produces pressure and facial pain
Fever and purulent discharge suggest bacterial etiology
Diagnosis is based on history, physical exam and, if necessary, sinus CT
Treatment includes antibiotic, decongestant and local measures
Severe complications: orbital cellulitis, subdural abscess, meningitis

pathophysiology: Infection or irritant causes inflammation of sinus mucosa
Inflamed mucosa produces edema and increases mucus viscosity
Obstruction of the ostium prevents drainage to the nasopharynx
Accumulation of secretions generates pressure and pain
If persistent, necrosis and extension to adjacent structures may occur
signs_symptoms: Localized facial pain (forehead, cheeks) worsened by leaning forward
Nasal congestion and thick (purulent or yellow) discharge
diagnostics: Physical exam: tenderness to palpation of sinuses
Purulent rhinorrhea and nasal mucosa edema
Sinus CT: opacification and mucosal thickening
CBC: leukocytosis with neutrophilia if bacterial
Nasal secretion culture only if resistant pathogen suspected
treatment: Broad‑spectrum antibiotic (e.g., amoxicillin, cefdinir) if bacterial suspected
Oral or topical decongestant (e.g., pseudoephedrine, oxymetazoline)
Analgesia: acetaminophen or ibuprofen for pain and fever
Nasal irrigation with isotonic saline solution
Topical nasal steroid (fluticasone) in chronic cases
nursing_care: Assess facial pain using a 0‑10 scale and locate sensitivity area
Monitor temperature and systemic infection signs
Maintain adequate hydration (≥ 2 L/day) to thin secretions
Position patient semi‑Fowler to aid drainage
Apply warm compresses to frontal/malar area 10‑15 min, 3‑4 times/day
patient_teaching: Perform nasal irrigation with saline twice daily
Avoid exposure to smoke, dust, and allergens
Complete the full antibiotic course even if symptoms improve
Use a humidifier in dry environments and rest adequately
Seek care if fever worsens, vision blurs, or ocular pain occurs

evidenced_by: pressure sensation in forehead and cheeks
outcomes: Reduced need for analgesics within 72 h

interventions.action: Administer analgesic per prescription and assess effect in 30 min
interventions.rationale: Control pain intensity and prevent inflammatory response

interventions.action: Apply warm compress to frontal/malar area 10‑15 min, 3‑4 times/day
interventions.rationale: Facilitates vasodilation and reduces sinus pressure

interventions.action: Teach patient relaxation techniques and PRN analgesic use
interventions.rationale: Promotes self‑management of pain and appropriate medication use

interventions.action: Reassess pain scale every 2 h and record changes
interventions.rationale: Allows adjustment of interventions and detection of improvement or deterioration

interventions.action: Maintain oral hydration of at least 2 L/day
interventions.rationale: Helps thin secretions and reduce irritation

outcomes: No signs of secondary infection within 7 days

interventions.action: Monitor temperature every 4 h and record values
interventions.rationale: Early detection of fever indicates possible secondary infection

interventions.action: Observe and describe amount and color of nasal discharge
interventions.rationale: Changes in discharge may signal infectious progression

interventions.action: Educate patient on importance of completing prescribed antibiotic
interventions.rationale: Prevents relapse and bacterial resistance

interventions.action: Instruct nasal hygiene with saline solution twice daily
interventions.rationale: Facilitates removal of pathogens and reduces colonization

interventions.action: Encourage avoidance of irritants (smoke, dust) and maintain humidified environment
interventions.rationale: Reduces mucosal irritation and infection risk

summary.0.quote: The medical diagnosis for inflamed sinuses that can be caused by a viral or bacterial infection is sinusitis . When the nasal membranes become swollen, the drainage of mucous is blocked and causes pain.

summary.1.quote: There are several types of sinusitis, including: Acute, which lasts up to 4 weeks Subacute, which lasts 4 to 12 weeks Chronic, which lasts more than 12 weeks and can continue for months or even years Recurrent, with several attacks within a year

key_points.0.quote: When the nasal membranes become swollen, the drainage of mucous is blocked and causes pain.

key_points.3.quote: Treatments include antibiotics, decongestants, and pain relievers.

sections.risk_factors.0.quote: Common causes of pharyngitis are the cold viruses, influenza, strep throat caused by group A streptococcus, and mononucleosis.

sections.risk_factors.1.quote: Allergies, nasal problems, and certain diseases can also cause acute and chronic sinusitis.

sections.risk_factors.2.quote: Assess the nasal septum for any deviation, perforation, or bleeding.

sections.risk_factors.3.quote: Nosebleeds can range from mild to more severe and can be caused by various factors, such as dry air, nasal trauma, nasal irrigation (such as allergies, sinus infections, exposure to irritants like smoke or chemicals), overuse of nasal decongestant sprays, blood-thinning medications (like aspirin , anticoagulants, and antiplatelets), nasal polyp s, hypertension, or foreign objects being inserted into the nose.

sections.signs_symptoms.3.quote: Symptoms of sinusitis can include fever, weakness, fatigue, cough, and congestion.

sections.signs_symptoms.4.quote: Nasal polyps can cause nasal congestion, difficulty breathing, and reduced sense of smell.

sections.diagnostics.0.quote: In cases of suspected sinusitis or sinus discomfort, gentle palpation can be applied to the sinus areas (forehead, cheeks) to check for tenderness, which can indicate inflammation.

sections.nursing_care.4.quote: Applying a cold compress to the nose and forehead can help constrict blood vessels and slow bleeding.
